ours.name: Northeast Buttress
ours.approach: Southbound on the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) down Bridge Creek, then northwest up North Fork Bridge Creek

fktText: Description At 9,199 feet, Goode is the tallest peak in the North Cascades and the eighth tallest peak in Washington State. Reached by crossing the Goode Glacier, the Northeast Buttress is a classic climbing route that features over 2,000 feet of mostly 3rd and 4th class climbing, with some 5th class mixed in. Most mountaineering parties complete the route in 2-3 days (the summit makes for a very nice bivy). The standard approach for the Northeast Buttress is via the Bridge Creek Trailhead on the North Cascades Highway (State Route 20). About 13 miles of flat and gradual downhill hiking brings you to an open area at the base of Goode. From here, it's about 5,800 feet of uphill gain to the summit. The descent is off the other side of the mountain, to the Park Creek Trail and back on the PCT at Bridge Creek—roughly 20 miles of well-maintained trail back to the Bridge Creek Trailhead. All told, this route includes about 33 miles of easy trail running (the majority on the PCT) and one large mountain climb. Goode can also be climbed from Stehekin, using a different approach to the same trail loop. ours.name: Fisher Chimneys
ours.approach: Park at the Lake Ann Trailhead on the east side of SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway), about 1 mile below Artist Point. Follow Lake Ann Trail #600, which immediately loses roughly 700-800 ft over its first ~1.7 miles through heather and blueberry slopes (a minor creek crossing near the low point), then climbs back about 1,000 ft over the final ~1.3 miles of switchbacks to the broad saddle above Lake Ann (about 4 miles and ~4,900-5,000 ft from the car). Just past the saddle is an unsigned junction: the right fork drops to Lake Ann's campsites and outlet — the last reliable water before the climb — while the left fork is the climber's boot path for Fisher Chimneys. ours.descent: Reverse the ascent line in its entirety. fktText: Description The Fisher Chimneys is an iconic trade route up Mt Shuksan in the North Cascades. Mt Shuksan is the 13th tallest mountain in the state and is guided via both the Sulphide Glacier, and the more technical Fisher Chimneys routes. The Fisher Chimneys route starts at the Lake Ann trailhead off highway 542. The first 5 miles meanders through pleasant valleys and by Lake Ann before turning up towards Shuksan. From here the route ascends a short section of 4th class scrambling to a boulder field, across the boulder field, and then up the chimneys. The chimneys consist of ~1200 vertical feet of 4th class scrambling in a stunning position. From the top of the chimneys, climbers ascend to 'Winnies Slide' which is a ~200ft tall snow embankment that eventually melts to glacial ice in the late summer. From here you pass through onto the Upper Curtis Glacier where you ascend then descend to the base of 'Hell's Highway which is a 300ft cornice like feature which requires front pointing to climb. Next comes a jaunt up the last bit of the Sulphide glacier to the summit pyramid. The summit pyramid involves sustained and exposed 4th class scrambling up a gully to the pointy summit. From here, one reverses the whole route back to the car. This popular route may see as many as 20 people climbing on a July weekend. ours.name: North Ridge (Complete)
ours.approach: Primary approach is from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached via Icicle Creek Road and FR 7601 out of Leavenworth). From the trailhead, follow the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail as it rolls along Mountaineer Creek through forest; at the signed junction roughly 2 miles in, stay right on the Stuart Lake Trail (the Colchuck Lake Trail is the left fork). Continue up the Mountaineer Creek valley on the Stuart Lake Trail, then leave the maintained trail before reaching Stuart Lake itself, cross Mountaineer Creek, and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. ours.descent: Nearly all parties descend via the Cascadian Couloir on the mountain's south side — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (0 rappels) under normal summer conditions. It is the only known way to climb 9 peaks of the Washington Bulgers 100 tallest list in a single day. ours.name: South Ridge / McAllister Glacier
ours.approach: Trailhead is the Eldorado Creek climbers' trailhead on Cascade River Road, roughly mile 20 out of Marblemount, at about 2,100 ft. From the parking pullout, backtrack a short distance downstream along the road to find a log or braided crossing of the North Fork Cascade River; ford/cross and pick up the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path on the far bank, angling up through heavy timber. This boot path is steep and root-laced, gaining roughly 1,800-1,900 ft through forest before breaking out at a boulder field around 4,000 ft; follow cairns and the intermittent trail on the right side of the talus (roughly 1,000 vertical ft of boulder-hopping) up into the open meadows of Eldorado Creek/El
ours.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down-climb the summit talus back to the North Klawatti Glacier, rope back up, and re-cross the glacier (same crevasse-probing caution as the approach) to the base of the McAllister-Klawatti notch. fktText: Description There are different interpretations of the famed " Inspiration Traverse " (depending of if you are climbing or ski'ing ) but upon reading multiple reports, for a car-to-car FKT style effort, the following is the most classic, desirable climber's line: Start from the Eldorado Trailhead and climb the 5 largest peaks of the traverse - Eldorado Peak (8,868') , Dorado Needle (8440') , Klawatti Peak (8485') , Austera Peak (8334') , and Primus Peak (8508') - before returning to the car. (an argument can be made for the point-to-point variation that exits out Thunder Creek, but the usual style for FKTs, especially considering the long car shuttle on this, is to do the car-to-car variations) the order the peaks are climbed is up to the FKT attempter. This is not a casual trail run . This route route has extensive crevassed glacier travel, steep snow, mid-5th class rock climbing, route finding, and exposed-high-risk terrain. Extensive experience with this skills is highly recommended before attempting. Planning for glacier conditions, weather, and day of the week (to avoid other parties) is a part of the logistics on this FKT. Be sure to read the route descriptions for the 4th/5th class terrain on Dorado, Klawatti, and Austera. You must tag the top of the true summit of each peak for this FKT to count...which on Dorado Needle includes a two move boulder problem that some describe as going at 5.7-5.9yds. ours.name: Northeast Couloir
ours.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail through the beaver meadows; at the first switchback past the meadows, beyond the Colchuck/Stuart Lake trail fork, leave the trail to the south on an obscure, unmaintained climbers' path, crossing Stuart Lake creek on logs, to reach the base of the northeast-facing couloir below Sherpa Peak. The path is unmaintained and can be hard to follow.
ours.descent: Most parties reverse the couloir (downclimbing or rappelling the snow/ice) back to the approach path. An alternative used by some parties is to traverse to Sherpa Pass and downclimb from there to regain camp, avoiding a full re-descent of the steepest snow.

ours.name: South Ridge
ours.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the El
ours.descent: Descend via Eldorado's standard East Ridge route back toward the glacier camp.

fktText: Description https://www.summitpost.org/eldorado-peak/150316 Eldorado Peak (8876') is Located in the North Cascades National Park and is on the Washington Top 100 list. Fred Beckey calls this peak "Queen of the Cascade River" considering that it is in the middle of a collection of beautiful peaks. Massively aloof, perched at the edge of the largest contiguous ice-sheet in the lower 48 states not connected to a volcano, the summit has a Himalayan like splendor owing to its remoteness, position, and knife-edge summit ridge. The total climb encompasses a 6,800 feet of vertical feet (not including ups and downs) and can be made through one of two interesting approaches. The climb is not technically difficult, and a number of people climb up each year to experience the thrill of stamping out a "just-wide-enough" path on the summit ridge and looking into the heart of the Klawatti-Inspiration-McAlister icecap. Views into Marble Creek, Dorado Needle, Forbidden Peak, Mount Buckner, Logan, Johannesburg and the other peaks of the Ptarmigan Traverse. It is an exhilarating summit experience, the ridge gives one a feeling of being out in the true alpine environment. This is a mountain that any mountaineer visiting the Pacific Northwest really should see and climb it! East Ridge : This is considered to be the Standard Route up Eldorado Peak because it has the lesser distance approach, the least amount of work, and is non technical. ours.name: SW Couloir and Face
ours.approach: Approach from Lake Ann; from below the Fisher Chimneys, traverse right (east) onto the Lower Curtis Glacier and follow it to the upper SE corner of the glacier basin below the couloir.
ours.descent: Descend as for the Fisher Chimneys route, via the Hourglass and Upper Curtis Glacier to the Shuksan Arm; round trip from Lake Ann is roughly 8 hours.

ours.name: Southwest Corner
ours.approach: Same approach as the South Face route to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft), then hike south toward the tower and ascend snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of the peak (roughly 6-8 hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead).
ours.descent: From the summit, downclimb the south face (Class 2-3) back to the col SW of the tower, then descend to Aasgard Pass and back down the loose talus/scree (or snow) to Colchuck Lake and the trailhead - roughly 1 hour from summit to the col.

ours.name: West Buttress
ours.approach: Same approach as the other routes: Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft), then the steep Aasgard Pass trail to the col behind Witches Tower; a steep snowfield crossing (ice axe recommended) leads to the route's base on the west side.
ours.descent: Descend via a combination of rappelling and downclimbing, including a notably exposed ledge traverse, back to the col/notch; from there, downclimb the steep snowfield (self-arrest position with ice axe) back toward Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the trailhead.
